title: Relation-Aware Graph Foundation Model
claim: Transfer across domains fails at the dataset and node levels, but succeeds when the shared relation is the transfer unit.
layout: Two circles left and right, central labeled arrows with ✗ and ✓ marks
description: Two large circles stand for two graph datasets: a blue Cora circle (Computer Science) on the left and a red Pubmed circle (Biomedicine) on the right. Each circle holds node icons of different shapes and symbols, linked by light-green glowing arrows that represent citation relations. A red arrow runs across the top between the circles with a big red X, labeled 'Dataset-level (Domain Gap)'. Two red arrows at the bottom also carry a red X, labeled 'Node-level (Heterogeneity)'. In the middle, a wide green curved double-headed arrow with a green check mark connects the two graphs, labeled 'Relation-level (Consistent Citation)'. The eye goes first to the green check and the red X marks, which set the failing transfer units against the working one.
caption: Comparison of transfer unit at the node, dataset, and relation levels.
abstract: In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capability to generalize across diverse natural language processing tasks, inspiring the development of graph foundation models (GFMs) for large-scale pre-training. However, unlike language models with explicit token units, graphs lack a well-defined unit for generalization, making it challenging to design effective pre-training strategies. In this work, we propose REEF, a novel GFM framework that leverages relation tokens as the fundamental units. We construct a vocabulary of relation tokens to encode relational information within graphs. To accommodate diverse relations, we introduce two hypernetworks that adaptively generate the parameters of aggregators and classifiers in graph neural networks based on relation tokens. In addition, we design another hypernetwork to construct dataset-specific projectors and incorporate a dataset-level feature bias into the initial node representations, enhancing flexibility across different datasets with the same relation. Extensive experiments demonstrate that REEF consistently outperforms existing methods in both pre-training and transfer learning, highlighting its potential as a general-purpose graph foundation model.
